1177.title: Taizé chant
1177.hook: a short line sung over and over until it sings you
1177.howItsDone: At Taizé, and in churches and student groups that borrow its style, prayer services center on short chants sung many times over, with scripture readings and a long silence, often by candlelight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the testimony service: people standing to tell what God has done. Your line was God has been good.

How many times can a person sing the same line before it stops being words? In a small village in France there's a monastic community called Taizé, brothers from different churches living under one rule. Young people travel there to stay for a week, and in the evening they crowd into a long, low-lit church and sit on the floor. There's no sermon to speak of. A few voices start a line, short enough to learn in one hearing, and everyone joins. Then again. And again. Somewhere along the way, some who sing it say, you stop singing the line and it starts singing you.

A Taizé chant is built small on purpose. One line, from scripture or an old prayer, set to a simple tune and sung over and over, sometimes with harmony underneath and a single voice rising above. The words come in Latin, in English, in other languages, so people who don't share a language can share a line. One chant sets the words of the thief crucified beside Jesus. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." That's the whole prayer. Sung slowly, many times, it has room to sink in. Now an objection some raise. Didn't Jesus say, in the King James words, "use not vain repetitions"? He did. The same verse says what he's warning against: those who "think that they shall be heard for their much speaking." Many readers, including those who sing at Taizé, take the problem to be the vain, not the repeated, and point to Matthew's own Gospel. In Gethsemane, on his last night, Jesus prays to let the cup pass, comes back, prays again, and then "prayed the third time, saying the same words." On his hardest night, he repeated himself. Here's why it can rest a person. When the line doesn't change, the mind can stop straining for the next word, or performing, or keeping up. The line carries you, the way a boat carries someone who has finally stopped rowing. And it can surface later, at a red light or over a sink full of dishes: a prayer that keeps going after the singing stops.

Choose a short line: if you pray, it could be the thief's, Lord, remember me; if not, any line that matters to you. Sing it quietly ten times on any simple tune, or just hum it, letting your fingers keep count, and if your mind wanders, simply come back to the line. After the tenth, stop, and let the quiet hold what's left.
Taizé chant. A short line of scripture or prayer, sung over and over, from a monastic community in France.
Your line: repetition is rest. Not vain words, just the same words, said again. Until tomorrow.

1178.title: Iona
1178.hook: a Scottish community on an old monastic island: worship, justice and work together
1178.howItsDone: Members of the Iona Community live in their own towns and cities, keep a shared rule of daily prayer and Bible reading, account to one another for their use of money and time, and commit to action for justice and peace; visitors join worship and common life at the abbey on Iona.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Taizé chant: one short line, sung until it sings you. Your line was repetition is rest.

A small island off the west coast of Scotland, wind and sheep and white sand. Tradition says an Irish monk named Columba landed here and built a monastery, and that for a very long time the island was a place of prayer. Much later, the old abbey stood roofless. Then a Glasgow minister named George MacLeod brought a strange crew out to the island: young ministers in training and out-of-work craftsmen. They rebuilt the abbey together, eating, praying and carrying stone side by side. Out of that work came a community that still bears the island's name.

The Iona Community isn't mainly people living on the island. Its members are scattered, living ordinary lives in cities and towns, and what holds them together is a shared rule. They keep daily prayer and Bible reading. They account to one another for how they spend their money and their time. They meet. And they commit to work for justice and peace. At Iona, prayer and politics aren't kept in separate rooms. The prayers there name wars, prisons, poverty and the earth. The conviction behind it reaches back to the prophets. Amos hears God speak to a people whose festivals were full while the poor were crushed in the courts: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols." And then: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Judgment there means justice, fair dealing in the courts. The worship was beautiful. The problem was everything outside it. Micah puts it briefly: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Christians weigh this differently. Some keep the church well away from politics, wary that faith gets used by one party or another. Others, like the Iona Community, hold that a prayer for peace that never touches how a city is run hasn't finished its sentence. Both want the gospel kept from being bent. They draw the line in different places.

Bring to mind one place far away where people are living through war or injustice, and hold it a while without rushing to fix it; then one place close to home, a street, a school, a courtroom, a shelter. If you pray, hold both before God with Amos's words, let judgment run down as waters. If you don't, hold both with care, and ask what one small act of fairness is within your reach.
Iona. An island off Scotland, and a scattered Christian community that keeps worship and the work of justice together.
Your line: prayer and politics. Justice, running down like water. Same time tomorrow.

1179.title: New monastics
1179.hook: people living near the poor with daily prayer and shared meals
1179.howItsDone: New monastic communities share a house or live near one another in struggling neighborhoods, keep a common rule with morning and evening prayer, share meals and resources, and open their tables to neighbors; members come from Protestant, Catholic and other churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Iona: worship and the work of justice kept in one rule. Your line was prayer and politics.

A row house on a block where cars rarely slow down. Inside, a handful of people share a kitchen, a budget and a prayer schedule. Before work, they pray around the table. In the evening the door is open, and a neighbor wanders in for soup and stays to talk. Nobody wears a habit. Nobody lives behind a wall. But they keep a rule, pray at set hours and share what they have, and they chose to live on this block on purpose, close to people who are struggling. Some people call them new monastics.

This block of the path has spent days with the old monastic families: Benedict's rule, the hours, the shared work. New monastics take that shape, a rule, set times of prayer, a common table, and plant it in ordinary neighborhoods instead of behind a cloister wall. They point back to the church's first days in Acts: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." Two chapters later Luke says it again: they "were of one heart and of one soul," and none of them called what he had his own. The other text they lean on is older. When the people of Judah were carried off to Babylon, other prophets were promising a quick return. Jeremiah sent them a letter instead: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." And then: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." The Hebrew word for peace there is shalom: wholeness, well-being. Settle in. Pray for the place. Your good is tied up with its good. Christians talk about the label in different ways. For some monks and nuns, monastic means vows and a monastery, and they'd keep the word for that. New monastics say they're borrowing old wisdom, not replacing it, and some keep close friendships with monasteries. Either way, the picture is plain: prayer, a table, and neighbors who come to dinner.
screen: `A RULE, THE HOURS, A SHARED TABLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people around you, next door, across the hall, down the street, and let one of them come forward. Set a simple table for them in your mind: soup, bread or takeout on paper plates, and where you'd sit. If you pray, pray for that neighbor by name, and for the peace of your street; if not, simply wish them well.
New monastics. Christians who keep a rule of daily prayer and shared meals in ordinary neighborhoods, often near people who are struggling.
Your line: monks among us. A rule, a table, an open door. See you tomorrow.

1180.title: Journaling and prayer walks
1180.hook: evangelicals who keep prayer journals and walk their streets praying for each house
1180.howItsDone: Some evangelical Christians keep a notebook of prayer requests and note later when and how they were answered; churches and small groups also organize prayer walks, walking a neighborhood slowly and praying for the homes, schools and businesses they pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new monastics: a rule, a shared table, and neighbors at dinner. Your line was monks among us.

A spiral notebook with a cracked cover, half full. Some pages are lists: a name, a diagnosis, a job interview, a daughter's exam. Next to a few of them, in different ink, written later, a date and one word: answered. Next to others, nothing yet. It's a prayer journal, and evangelical Christians are among those who keep them. Some of them also take the notebook in a pocket and walk their own street slowly, praying for each house they pass. Two habits, one on paper and one on foot.

Start with the paper. When the prophet Habakkuk waits for God's answer, the answer begins: "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it." Write it down, plainly, so it can be carried. The Psalms themselves are written prayers, complaint and praise on the same page. In one of them, the writer is so troubled he can't sleep, and then he turns: "I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old." That's what a prayer journal is for. Memory is slippery, and a page isn't. Months later you can read what you were afraid of, see what happened, and see how your own prayers changed. Now the feet. Genesis gives Enoch one short line: "And Enoch walked with God." A life with God, pictured as a walk. Prayer walkers take the picture outdoors. They go slowly, eyes open, and let what they see become the prayer. A swing set: the children on this street. A for-sale sign: whoever's leaving, and whoever's coming. A wheelchair ramp. A window that stays dark. Matthew says that when Jesus went through the towns and saw the crowds, "he was moved with compassion on them." He saw first. Walking slowly is a way of seeing. Some people bring the two habits together. They walk, come home and write down the houses they prayed for, and later, sometimes, what happened.

If you're able, stand and walk, outside or slowly around the room; if you're sitting, walk your street in your mind, one house at a time. Notice one detail at each, a car, a toy, a porch light, and let it become the prayer. If you pray, ask God's good for whoever lives there; if you don't, simply wish them well.
Journaling and prayer walks. Prayers written down to be remembered, and prayers walked, house by house, with eyes open.
Your line: pray as you walk. Eyes open, house by house. Rest well.

1181.title: Block close: find your way
1181.hook: many doors into prayer, all opening to the same house
1181.tomorrow: Love, and do what you will
1181.howItsDone: In Christian practice, a rule of prayer is something kept over time: a daily office, a rosary or prayer rope, a quiet time with the Bible, a weekly prayer meeting, sometimes with guidance from a pastor, priest or spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday, journaling and prayer walks: prayers on paper and on foot. Your line was pray as you walk.

Luke has already shown Jesus slipping away into the wilderness to pray, and once spending all night in prayer on a mountain. Then one day, "as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased," one of them asks: "Lord, teach us to pray." Not teach us about prayer. Teach us to do it. This whole block has walked through a house of prayer, room after room, each furnished by a different family of Christians. Today there's no new room, just a practical question: of all the doors you've opened, which one will you keep using?

Walk back through the rooms. The Benedictines: listen, the hours, the kitchen rota, tools treated like altar vessels. The Orthodox way of the heart: the mind brought down into the heart, watchfulness at the door, the prayer rope. The Franciscans, with brother and sister creatures. The Carmelites, with Teresa's four ways to water a garden and God among the pots and pans. The Ignatian way: imagine the scene, notice consolation and desolation. Celtic blessings for everything. Anglican morning and evening prayer. Luther's advice to his barber, Reformed psalms and family worship. Anabaptist yieldedness, Quaker silence, Methodist class meetings, a covenant renewed. And lately, louder rooms: hands raised in praise, a hand on a shoulder, a word weighed, bold prayer for the sick, the preacher calling and the people answering, testimony, a Taizé line sung over and over, Iona's prayers for justice, a shared table, a notebook and a walk. None of these was invented as a sampler. Each belongs to a community and a whole life of faith, meant to be kept, not tried once. Benedict asked his monks to promise stability: stay put, and let the place shape you. In John's Gospel, Jesus says: "Abide in me, and I in you." Abide means stay, remain, keep living there. And when the disciples asked to be taught, Luke records no catalog of methods. Jesus said, "When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven," one prayer to keep. So the block ends with a choice. Not the best way. Your way, for now: one door you'll walk through every day this month, until it feels like a room you live in.

Let the rooms of this block drift past without judging them, and notice which one you keep coming back to. Choose that one, and make it small and concrete: when, where, and for how long; five minutes is plenty. If you pray, you can offer the choice to God.
Block close. The end of the block on traditions of prayer: many rooms walked through, and one way chosen to keep.
Your line: one way, kept. One door, until it feels like home. Tomorrow, a new block begins: living it.

1182.title: Love, and do what you will
1182.hook: Augustine's line: love, then do what you want, because love will guide it
1182.howItsDone: Some Christian teachers quote Augustine's "love, and do what you will" when teaching that love of God and neighbor is the heart of the moral life, and some preachers pair it with Paul's words that love is the fulfilling of the law.

segments.voice: Yesterday was the block close on prayer: many doors, one house. Your line was one way, kept. Today a new block opens: living it, Christian ethics.

"Love, and do what thou wilt." That's a bishop talking. Augustine is preaching through the first letter of John, a short letter that keeps circling back to one word, and in the middle of a sermon he folds the whole moral life into one short command. Do what you want? From a bishop? It sounds like a permission slip, and it can be quoted like one: to excuse a shortcut, a betrayal, a cruelty that felt honest at the time. In its place, it means something much harder.

Look at what Augustine is talking about when he says it. Not doing whatever feels good: correction. In the same sermon he sets two scenes side by side. A father disciplines his son, and it looks harsh. A kidnapper is gentle with a child he has stolen, and it looks kind. Which one loves? You can't tell from the outside. You have to look at the root: the same act can grow from love or from something else entirely. Then comes the line, and right after it, the examples. If you keep silent, keep silent out of love. If you speak up, speak up out of love. If you correct, correct out of love. If you spare, spare out of love. Augustine isn't inventing this. He's reading the letter in front of him: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God." And Paul, writing to Rome, lists the commandments, do not kill, do not steal, and says they're all summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself: "love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." So the rules aren't thrown out. They're gathered up. Over the coming days the path walks through the commandments one at a time, and Augustine's line is the lens: each rule is what love looks like in one corner of life. In his sermon, love isn't a warm mood. It wants the other person's real good, even when that costs you their approval. That makes it a stricter test than any rule, not a looser one.
screen: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one decision waiting for you, a reply you owe, a no you're dreading, a correction you might give, and ask Augustine's question: what's at the root here, love for this person, or fear, or pride, or wanting to be liked? Don't decide yet; just look at the root, honestly. If you pray, you can hold the choice before God in silence.
Love. In Augustine's line, the root every act should grow from: wanting the other person's real good, whether that means speaking up or staying quiet.
Your line: love decides. Stricter or gentler, the act follows the root. See you tomorrow.

1183.title: Numbering the commandments
1183.hook: Catholics and Lutherans number them one way, Orthodox and Reformed another; the words are the same
1183.howItsDone: Christians learn the Ten Commandments in catechism, Sunday school and confirmation classes, and each tradition teaches its own numbering: Catholic and Lutheran catechisms one way, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican teaching another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine: love, and do what you will, with every act checked at the root. Your line was love decides.

Ask a few Christians to recite the second commandment, and you may get two different answers, each said with total confidence. One says: no graven images. Another says: don't take the Lord's name in vain. Neither has misremembered. They grew up in churches that count differently. Catholics and Lutherans number the commandments one way. Orthodox and Reformed Christians number them another. Day 394 walked through the ten words themselves; today, why the Bible lets the counting differ.

Open Exodus 20 and look for the numbers. There aren't any. The passage runs from "I am the LORD thy God" to the warning about coveting your neighbor's house, wife, servants, ox and donkey, as one unbroken speech. What the Bible does give is the total. Later in Exodus, the tablets carry "the words of the covenant, the ten commandments." In the Hebrew, that phrase reads, literally, the ten words, which is today's line. So: ten. But where do the cuts go? Catholics and Lutherans, following a division tradition credits to Augustine, keep no other gods and no carved images together as the first word, then split coveting in two at the end: your neighbor's wife, then your neighbor's goods. Orthodox and Reformed Christians, and Anglicans with them, make images a word of its own and keep coveting together as the last. Jewish tradition counts another way again: its first word is God's own introduction, I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt. Each pattern underlines something. Setting images apart puts weight on how God is worshipped. Splitting coveting, some readers say, makes clear that a person is not a possession. Starting with I am says the law begins with who God is and what God has done, before any rule. Whichever way a church counts, every word is still read. The words on the tablets are the same words; only the dividing lines move.

If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read Exodus 20, the first seventeen verses, slowly, once, without numbering anything; just notice where you'd put the breaks. If the text isn't to hand, say the ones you remember, in whatever order they come, and notice which come to you first.
Numbering the commandments. The same ten words, divided in different places by different churches, with every word kept.
Your line: ten words. That's a week, from Taizé's repeated chant through Iona, new monastics and prayer walks, to Augustine's love and the ten words. I'll be here tomorrow.

fork.setup: you're dividing Exodus 20 into ten. you reach the end: don't covet your neighbor's house, wife, servants, ox or donkey. one word, or two?
options: one word: coveting is one desire.
two words: a person and a possession are different.
either one: the text gives no numbers.
fork.reveal: Exodus gives no numbers. Orthodox and Reformed Christians keep coveting as one word; Catholics and Lutherans make it two. both read every word.

chat.says: My church says the second commandment is about images. Yours says God's name. Which Bible is wrong?
options: Neither. The words are the same; churches just draw the lines between the ten in different places.
Neither. Each church left out a different commandment, so both lists come up a little short.
Yours. Exodus 20 prints a number beside each one, so the other church simply misread the list.
chat.meaning: Exodus 20 has no numbers. The Bible gives the total, ten, and churches divide the same words differently, keeping every word.
